clue.text: Jump on horse and get going

blocks.note: to start is to jump in surprise
a rider on a horse is said to be up

explanation.surface: A rider leaps into the saddle and sets off.
explanation.walkthrough: A jockey who is riding is 'up', as in the racecard phrase 'Dettori up'.
explanation.definitionFit: To start up is a phrasal verb meaning to begin moving or set something in motion.

clue.text: Striking gesture

blocks.note: first meaning: notable or conspicuous, as in a notable success
second meaning: a movement made to convey a message

explanation.walkthrough: Read together the words suggest a blow or a dramatic movement; the adjective sense, as in 'a signal victory', is the less familiar one.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an adjective meaning remarkable or outstanding and a noun for a sign made to communicate.

clue.text: One who may appear in a flash

definitions.text: One who may appear in a flash

blocks.clueFragment: One who may appear in a flash
blocks.note: surface reading: someone who pops up suddenly, in an instant
setter's reading: a news flash, the brief bulletin read out on radio or television by a presenter

explanation.walkthrough: 'In a flash' is an idiom for very quickly, but here a flash is a news flash, and the person who appears in one reads it.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadcaster who reads out news bulletins on radio or television is the person heard or seen in a newsflash.

clue.text: Fuss about river exercise creating danger to shipping

indicators.note: the word for a fuss goes about, or around, the river and exercise letters

blocks.note: a to-do is a fuss or commotion
R is the standard abbreviation for river
PE is physical education, school exercise

explanation.surface: A commotion over some activity on a river that threatens passing boats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exercise' here is the school-subject abbreviation, physical education; the fuss splits around the river and exercise letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A self-propelled underwater missile fired at vessels is a weapon that threatens ships at sea.

clue.text: Sounds like affectionate donkey's given bedding

indicators.note: the phrase tells us the answer is said the same as the words that follow, though spelt differently

blocks.note: pally means friendly or affectionate
an ass is a donkey

explanation.surface: A fond donkey has been handed some straw to sleep on.
explanation.walkthrough: PALLY ASS spoken aloud gives the old word for a straw mattress, spelt PALLIASSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A palliasse is a straw-filled mattress, a basic kind of bed covering or bedding for sleeping on.

clue.text: Amounts expressed numerically as squares, say

blocks.note: first meaning: numbers given as digits
second meaning: geometric shapes, of which a square is one example

explanation.surface: Square numbers being written out as digits in a maths lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Squares' seems to continue the arithmetic theme of square numbers, but it is an example of shapes.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both numerical values or digits and geometric shapes such as triangles, circles and squares.

clue.text: Entrance hall designed to meet needs of the old within

indicators.note: the old word sits within the word for 'designed to meet needs of'

blocks.note: something made for a person is designed to serve them
ye is an archaic form of the, as in 'Ye Olde Tea Shoppe'

explanation.surface: A lobby laid out to suit elderly visitors inside a building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The old' looks like elderly people, but it means the archaic spelling of 'the', as on olde-worlde shop signs.
explanation.definitionFit: A foyer is the lobby or reception area just inside the entrance to a theatre, hotel or block of flats.

clue.text: So-called farmer briefly in charge of agricultural work

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the farmer's name loses its final letter

blocks.note: the name George comes from the Greek for farmer or earth-worker
IC is the abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: A farmer, as he is known, has been put temporarily in charge of the farming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'So-called' signals a name: George is Greek for farmer. Virgil's Georgics are poems about farming.
explanation.definitionFit: A georgic is a poem on farming and rural life, a literary work about agriculture, like Virgil's Georgics.

clue.text: Take to the streets and dance around Bull's Head

indicators.note: the dance goes around the letter taken from the bull
the head of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: a reel is a lively Scottish dance
the first letter of Bull

explanation.surface: Protesters march and dance round a statue of a bull's head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bull's Head' looks like a pub name, but it means only the first letter of Bull.
explanation.definitionFit: To rebel is to rise up against authority, and protesting in public on the streets is one form of that.

clue.text: Wise man keeping jug for removal of water

indicators.note: the wise man keeps, or holds, the jug inside himself

blocks.note: a sage is a wise man
a ewer is a large water jug

explanation.surface: A sage holds on to a jug meant for carrying water away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For removal of water' reads as the jug's purpose, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sewerage is the system of drains and pipes that carries waste water away from buildings.

clue.text: Senior officer likely to appear heartless in most cases

indicators.note: with its heart removed only the outside letters of likely are left

blocks.note: a general is a senior army officer
the first and last letters of likely

explanation.surface: A high-ranking officer who will probably come across as unfeeling.
explanation.definitionFit: Generally is an adverb meaning usually or as a rule, true of the majority of instances.

clue.text: Bend in river in neat part of London

blocks.note: neat is an old word for cattle, so an ox is a neat
Bow is a district in the East End of London

explanation.surface: A curve in the Thames running through a tidy London district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neat' looks like an adjective for tidy, but it is the archaic noun for cattle. Bow is an East London district, home of the Bow Bells.
explanation.definitionFit: An oxbow is a U-shaped loop or meander in a river's course, which can later become a lake.

clue.text: American imprisoned by Lincoln for insulting language

indicators.note: something imprisoned is shut inside its captor

blocks.note: Abe is Abraham Lincoln's short name
US is short for the United States, so American

explanation.surface: An American is jailed by President Lincoln for swearing.
explanation.walkthrough: ABE holds US: AB + US + E.
explanation.definitionFit: Abuse means rude, offensive or insulting words directed at someone, as in shouting abuse.

clue.text: Not even one of the Baker Street boys, for example

definitions.text: one of the Baker Street boys, for example

blocks.note: first meaning: uneven or not uniform

blocks.clueFragment: one of the Baker Street boys, for example
blocks.note: second meaning: a member of the street urchins who helped Sherlock Holmes

explanation.walkthrough: Sherlock Holmes lived at 221B Baker Street and used a gang of street boys, the Baker Street Irregulars, as spies; 'for example' allows any irregular.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an adjective for uneven or unsymmetrical, and a noun for a member of an unofficial band.

clue.text: Oppose the production of chickens -- a very shady activity

blocks.note: to cross someone is to oppose them
chicks are produced by eggs hatching

explanation.surface: Objecting to poultry farming, which is presented as something dodgy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shady' suggests underhand dealing, but it means literally creating shade in a drawing.
explanation.definitionFit: Cross-hatching is drawing two sets of crossing parallel lines to make shading in an illustration.

clue.text: Game player in a loose scrum is dumbfounded

indicators.note: the player is placed in the middle of the scrum phrase

blocks.note: a ruck is a loose scrum in rugby, formed round the ball on the ground
West is one of the four players at bridge, a card game

explanation.surface: A rugby player buried in a ruck is left stunned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game player' suggests a rugby player, but the game is bridge, whose four players are named for compass points.
explanation.definitionFit: Awestruck means filled with wonder or amazement, so stunned into silence like someone dumbfounded.

clue.text: Realise it is wrong for this old citizen

indicators.note: if the letters are wrong, they are in the wrong order and must be rearranged

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone realises a mistake about an elderly citizen.
explanation.definitionFit: An Israelite was a member of the ancient Hebrew nation, an inhabitant of the old kingdom of Israel.

clue.text: It's delivered by hand to striker not working with the rest

definitions.text: It's delivered by hand to striker

blocks.note: a machine that is off is not working
a break is a rest from work

explanation.surface: A letter hand-delivered to a worker on strike, who is off taking time out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Striker' suggests a picket, but in cricket the striker is the batsman facing the bowler. 'By hand' points to finger spin.
explanation.definitionFit: An off-break is a spinning cricket ball bowled with a twist of the fingers that turns toward the batsman.

clue.text: Looking at other people's hands, one knows what's on the cards

definitions.text: Looking at other people's hands, one knows what's on the cards

blocks.clueFragment: Looking at other people's hands, one knows what's on the cards
blocks.note: surface reading: a card player who cheats by peeking at opponents' hands and so knows the cards held
setter's reading: palms are read for clients, and tarot cards show what is in store

explanation.walkthrough: 'On the cards' is an idiom for likely to happen, and palm reading is studying hands; both are a seer's trade.
explanation.definitionFit: A clairvoyant who reads palms and tarot cards claims to predict what lies in the future for clients.

clue.text: Such work lacks order and is not called for

blocks.note: first meaning: a book without page numbers, so with nothing to fix its sequence
second meaning: not summoned over a loudspeaker or bleeper

explanation.walkthrough: The second half reads as 'unnecessary', but it means literally not having been called by a pager.
explanation.definitionFit: A book with no numbered leaves has no fixed sequence, and a person nobody has summoned by tannoy has not been paged.

clue.text: Article put on line, wet, here?

definitions.text: Article put on line, wet, here?

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for line
a is the indefinite article
something wet is not dry

explanation.surface: A garment pegged out damp on a washing line.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'put on' places the article after L. Read whole, the clue also describes the place where clothes are washed and hung out.
explanation.definitionFit: A laundry is a room or business where clothes and linen are washed, then hung up to dry.

clue.text: A Degas reproduction more than one saw

indicators.note: a reproduction remakes the original, so its letters are made again in another order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A copy of a Degas painting, seen by several people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like the past tense of see, but it is a noun: a saying.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is an old proverb, so several saws are traditional sayings or proverbs.

clue.text: Obscene publication's original plan

blocks.note: a blue joke or film is indecent
a print is something published

explanation.surface: The first draft of a pornographic magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: A blueprint is a technical drawing for a building or machine, hence any initial design or scheme.

clue.text: Marry single sweetheart

indicators.note: this word splits in two, and its second half, heart, asks for only the central letter of the first half

blocks.note: a unit is a single thing
the central letter of sweet

explanation.surface: Wed an unattached darling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweetheart' reads as one word, a lover, but splits into sweet and heart.
explanation.definitionFit: To unite is to join together, and to marry is to join two people in wedlock.

clue.text: Gather inside train ferry

indicators.note: the answer is found inside the run of letters across the next words

blocks.note: the letters across the word break

explanation.surface: Assembling inside a ferry that carries trains.
explanation.definitionFit: To gather can mean to understand or conclude from evidence, as in 'I gather you're leaving'.

clue.text: Drastically affect with revolting object

blocks.note: people up in arms are in revolt
an end is an aim or object

explanation.surface: Something disgusting can have a severe effect on you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolting' suggests disgusting, but means rising in revolt; 'object' is a purpose, not a thing.
explanation.definitionFit: To upend is to turn upside down, hence to overturn or radically disrupt someone's life or plans.

clue.text: Contemplating year one had in England

indicators.note: the year and one are held in the abbreviation for the country

blocks.note: Eng is the abbreviation for England
Y is short for year
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Thinking over a year someone spent in England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Had in' means held inside; this is the less common spelling, also written eyeing.
explanation.definitionFit: Eying is looking at something carefully, weighing it up with the eyes in a considering way.

clue.text: Tom Jones, for one, came across the heath

blocks.note: to come across something is to find it
ling is heather, the plant of heathland

explanation.surface: The singer Tom Jones walked across the moor.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom Jones is not the Welsh singer but Fielding's novel hero, a baby abandoned and found.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Fielding's Tom Jones is an abandoned infant raised by Squire Allworthy, an example of a deserted child.

clue.text: One working to make dough sounds like poor person

indicators.note: the phrase says the answer is pronounced like the words that follow

blocks.note: a needy person, one in need

explanation.surface: Someone toiling to earn money is called a pauper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make dough' reads as earning money, but it is bread-making.
explanation.definitionFit: A kneader works bread dough by pressing and folding it with the hands, so is preparing dough.

clue.text: Without a clue, don't enter so much data

blocks.note: to key data is to type or enter it
read with 'so much', don't do so much means do less
surface padding completing the phrase; 'so much' pairs with don't and data is what is keyed

explanation.surface: Clueless advice: input less information.

explanation.definitionFit: A key is an explanation or solution, so lacking one means having no guide or answer.
